historyTimelineInfo:
before 1987: had a kids activity sheet with no reward
It is guessed that the junior ranger book before 2009 started in early 2000
2009: Our current Junior Ranger program has been in service since 2009 when we redesigned our activity book with an NPS grant funded by the NPS Foundation. The Junior Ranger Activity book was designed by our park's staff and volunteers. the development of the book took two years and involved collecting examples from around the NPS and using local artist and SCA intern to develop the artwork. All the actives in the book were designed by the staff and partner with local teachers to meet the demands of state education standards.
2010: After the books completion we submitted it to the 2010 NAI conference where it won the interpretive media award for that year.
Around 2011: reprinted the book with slight changes
Over the years we have also used the Junior Paleontologist program, The Junior Space program, and the Southeastern Archaeology Center (SEAC) Junior Ranger programs. We have handed out those program badges to visitors in the past.
2018: they discontinued their plastic badge when the company that supplied them closed. At the time we switched to an all-wooden badge from a new supplier.
2018: we started the Junior Ranger Summer Day Camp and De Soto Fishing Rancho programs. It was decided at the time to develop Junior Ranger badges for those two programs as well. The purpose was to increase participation and to make both these programs unique with their own badges.
2019: we came up with the concept of creating the Master Junior Ranger Program. This program rewards visitors who complete our Junior Ranger book, participate in a fishing rancho, and attend three-day camp programs. When a Junior Ranger completes all our programs, they show the park staff their badges and they then receive our Master Junior Ranger Challenge Coin.
Since we have created our Master Junior Ranger Program, we have no plans of developing a Citizen Ranger program at this time.

historyTimelineInfo:
:
1965:
Since the founding of Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area in 1965, there has always been a Junior Ranger like Program.
1978:
The oldest known program was created 1978, named Discovering Delaware Water Gap: A Field Guide for Young Naturalists. While some phrases in the book are no longer used, and many activities no longer permissible (please don’t dig, crush, or take home the nature!), the book is still available to take home.
1990s:
This book was used until the 1990’s, when the program received a massive reboot. Several junior ranger programs were released in English and Spanish and featured unique patches and later - pencils. There was even a Senior Ranger Program! Unfortunately, except for Junior Ranger Naturalist (English and Spanish) and Junior Ranger Explorer (English), which are found in park archives, park staff can no longer locate the programs, patches, or pencils used.
2010:
the unique park-specific junior ranger programs were streamlined into one “Junior Ranger Activity Book”, which would earn you the park badge. Around this time the park began offering additional Junior Ranger Programs including: “Adventure Guide For Teens: The Appalachian Trail in Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area” (discontinued), “Junior Ranger Let's Go Fishing!”, “Junior Night Explorer”, “Junior Ranger River Safety Activity Book”, and scout specific programs.
The newest version of the park’s junior ranger program is part of a colorful newspaper-style publication called “Kids Guide to the Gap”. In a throwback to the 90’s, there are six different junior ranger programs one could complete to earn the park badge, with something special if one completes all six.
2020: They had 3000 junior rangers.

2007-2010: The first Junior Ranger book was created while the plans for the permanent memorial were being developed.

2017: Discontinued their plastic badge and switched to a wooden badge featuring the 'Tower of Voices' one of the locations within the memorial. It took some time to cycle through the badges as they still had plastic summer 2019
April 2021: The collaborative "Western Pennsylvania Virtual Junior Ranger" program was launched. This was created similar to the 5 park centennial patch but had no special award.
2021:  Flight 93 piloted an in-person Junior Ranger Program during the summer months. It's a 75 minute program at the memorial with a ranger and participants complete the program and are sworn in.

historyTimelineInfo:
:
1982: There was a children's activity book entitled "Exploring Fort Necessity" published in technically it was not a "Junior Ranger" program, it filled the same niche.
Prior to 1989: An in-house 5.5" x 8.5" Jr. Ranger booklet was produced for children 6-12 yrs. old. Participant were given a plastic badge for completing a number of exercises appropriate for their age.
In September 2006, the in-house booklet was replaced with an 8.5" x 11" booklet. The work was done primarily by an intern through the Junior Ranger Ambassadors Program.
2016: switched over to the wooden badges, phased out the plastic badges.
2016: had a special patch for the centennial, parks of western PA. There was one patch that you got after you completed the junior ranger program at all 5 parks, Friendship hill, Fort necessary, Flight 93, Johnston Flood, and  Allagany portage railroad.
April 2021: The collaborative "Western Pennsylvania Virtual Junior Ranger" program was launched. This was created similar to the 5 park centennial patch but had no special award.
June 2021: Fort Necessity debuted a Advance Jr. Ranger booklet, targeted for visitors 13 and up.

siteInfo:
To become a Gettysburg junior ranger ask for the Free junior ranger Activity book at the information desk in the Visitor Center.
Complete at least three of the seven activities in the booklet during your day at the park. These activities include completing answers to questions about exhibits in the Museum of the Civil War at the park Visitor Center, questions about the Gettysburg Address and President Lincoln’s visit to dedicate the Soldiers' National Cemetery, describe a ranger-guided program that you attend, answer puzzles from your tour of the battlefield and proivde short answers about some of the many monuments in the park.
Return the booklet to the information desk where a park ranger will review your book with you. If you have successfully completed three of the activities, you’ll receive a patch and certificate making you a Junior Ranger at Gettysburg National Military Park!

To become a Jewel Cave junior ranger, stop by the visitor center to request an junior ranger activity booklet or email them to request a mailed copy.
For a certificate:
- Ages 5-6:      2 booklet activities
- Ages 7-9:      4 booklet activates
- Ages 10-12:  6 booklet activities
For a certificate and Badge:
 - Ages 5-6:
     4 booklet activities, attend 1 Ranger Program
 - Ages 7-9:
     6 booklet activities, attend 1 Ranger program
 - Ages 10-12:
      8 booklet activities, attend 1 Ranger program
For a certificate, badge, patch:
- Ages 5-6:
   6 booklet activities, attend 2 Ranger Programs
- Ages 7-9:
  8 booklet activities, attend 2 Ranger Programs
- Ages 10-12:
  10 booklet activities, attend 2 Ranger Programs
Ranger programs are a requirement to receive the badge a patch so that visitors to Jewel Cave do not use the booklet in lieu of interpretive programming. Formal programs: patio talks, guided walks, and cave tours. We also consider watching the park film and completion of scavenger hunt in visitor center to be programs as well.
Completion would probably take anywhere from approximately 30 minutes to an hour depending on age and what level of completion they want.
*Scroll down if in google maps to see info there is a bug showing this as a second info area instead of last.**.
In 2016 and 2017 JECA also developed and ran a Junior Caver Ranger (originally Junior Spelunking Ranger) for those aged 9-15. These tours seem similar to our Wild Caving tour which takes those 18+ (16-17 with parent permission) on a more authentic caving experience that requires climbing, crawling, and squeezing through passageways.
The Junior Caver Program involves participants learning surveying techniques and completing a Junior Caver Booklet as they go through the cave. Completion of the program awarded a JECA unique “Junior Cave Ranger” patch. Per the tour rack card, the program was free.
This program seems to only have run from June-August in 2016 and 2017. signed waivers indicate that nine people participated in 2016 and three in 2017. These waivers were signed in September, which is outside of the tour time range on the rack card.

historyTimelineInfo:
Broken Down Timeline of Junior Ranger/Similar Programs
1988: No Junior Ranger program existed at JECA
1997-1999: JECA’s non-profit partner provided a small amount funding for Junior Ranger Materials, about $100 each of those years. This is not enough for a complete program, perhaps these were for pilot materials.
1999: Annual report suggest that JECA had 4,700 Junior Ranger participants. It is unclear what exactly participation consisted of.
2000: Interpretive staff at JECA developed two Junior Ranger Booklets (one for ages 5-8 and one for ages 9-12). A badge was developed at this time as well. This is the earliest date suggesting an official booklet and program.
2001: Booklets are tested one weekend with 35 participants. Unclear if participants received anything in exchange.
2002: Booklets are tested one weekend with 88 participants. Free cave tours were offered in exchange for feedback if families had two or more children. Additional 3,675 books were handed out.
2002: Book was apparently redesigned, perhaps using feedback from test weekends.
2003: A Junior Ranger weekend was tested for the new books. Additionally they handed out 4,031 junior rangers books
 2004: They handed out 4,510 junior ranger books.
2005: Physical copy of booklet from 2005 exists at JECA visitor center. They handed out 6,580 books this year.
2006: They handed out 3,770 junior ranger books.
2007: Booklet was updated, but failed to address various learning and developmental levels. They handed out 3,615 junior ranger books.
2008: They handed out 3,875 junior ranger books.
2009: They handed out 4,609 junior ranger books.
2010: New Junior Ranger booklet was unveiled with age groups broken up and tiered requirements for completion. They handed out 6,879 of them.
2011: Pee Wee ranger program is launched with 375 participants this year. They handed out 4,186 regular junior ranger books.
 2013: They gave out 4,876 junior ranger books.
2014: they developed a new junior ranger book in the summer of 2014, starting on June 20th with a final draft being completed by September 1st. This book was first printed in 2015. This Junior ranger booklet was updated by seasonal interpretive rangers. They gave out 4,689 junior ranger books.
2015: New Junior Ranger booklet was first printed. They handed out 5,158 junior ranger books.
2016: They gave out 8,700 junior ranger books.
2016-2017: Junior Cave Ranger program is launched with what seems to be only twelve  participants(more below). They gave out 8,663 junior ranger books.
2017: They gave out 8,663 junior ranger books
2018:   They gave out 7,845 books; 7,293 badges
 2019:  They gave out 7,562 books; 6,787 badges
 2020:   They gave out books 1,800 books; 2,000 badges
2021 (present): No known changes have been made to the Junior Ranger booklet since

The card will be punched at each subsequent visit by the Junior Ranger candidate when he/she attends a State Parks-sponsored nature program or history program. siteName: Missisquoi National Wildlife Refuge Admin Building And Visitor
Mississippi National River and Recreation Area
siteInfo:
To become a Mississippi River junior ranger they currently have 2 options for earning a standard ‘Freddy’ (our fish mascot) badge at our Mississippi River Visitor Center.
1. We have a booklet that coincides with the exhibits at the Mississippi River Visitor Center, and can only be completed at the visitor center.
2.We also have a Family Tree walks booklet that takes JRs outside to explore the tree communities we have outside of the visitor center. This takes about an hour, and is best done in spring, summer, or fall.
Other ways to be a junior ranger at the visitor center
-You can pick up a third larger JR Activity Booklet,that is available in person, or can be mailed out/ sent via email by requesting a copy through our ‘email the Junior Ranger Coordinator’ link at www.nps.gov/thingstodo/earn-a-junior-ranger-badge.htm.
Completion of this larger booklet earns one of the new Mississippi National River and Recreation Area wooden badges.
-they also have national booklet versions and badges--Let's Go Fishing, Underwater Explorer, Night Sky, Paleontology, and Historic Preservation. Railroad Explorer is also available. (RRE doesn't have a badge that goes with it.)
The MRVC booklet takes about 30 min. The Tree Walk, about an hour. The larger Activity book might take an hour, depending on how many age-based activities the JR does. Earning a JR badge at St. Anthony Falls means taking a tour or doing some self-guided learning…30 min or less.
specialPrograms: Historic Preservation | Junior Angler | Night Explorer | Railroad Explorer | Underwater Explorer

historyTimelineInfo:
In 1978 new river gorge national park was established.
early 1990s:
They first created a simple, single-color activity booklet of 16 - 20 pages to help kids learn more about this park. You would earn a patch with the completion of the book.
Law enforcement would also hand out plastic badges to kids doing good deeds.
mid/late 1990s:
NERI interpretive rangers started giving youth the choice to earn either the patch OR badge by completing the Junior Ranger booklet
Around 2000:
NERI interpretive rangers revised the park's in-classroom, curriculum-based educational program, with a different course taught by rangers in schools for each grade. School students that went through this program earned a NERI Junior Ranger sticker after they completed their 5th grade level program with a park ranger. This sticker was for this curriculum program only, so was not handed out in association with the JR booklet.
After 2000:
NERI Interpretive rangers would conduct Junior Ranger programs periodically during the busy summer season and sometimes with school groups. In these programs youth could work on their Junior Ranger booklet with a NERI ranger and earn their patch OR badge by the end of these special programs.
Around 2010:
 we completely revised the NERI's Junior Ranger booklet, now a full color with 24-page.
This new Junior Ranger booklet was designed to be completed by people ages 5 years old and up; some adults like to compete/earn the Junior Ranger booklet too. Several of the activities in the booklet are designed to be completed while visiting this park site.
December 2020: became a national park
early 2021:
NERI developed a new addition to the park's Junior Ranger program, a Junior Junior Ranger booklet. This booklet is targeted toward younger kids ages 2 to 5 yrs. By completing this four-page booklet, little kids can earn the NEW Junior Junior Ranger sticker.
2021:
along with the new national park title, they have new plastic junior ranger badges and won’t order new patches at the moment, and will let the current ones run out.
around 2023:
Their next order of Junior ranger badges might be wooden to go with trends
2021: they had over 3,000 junior rangers

description:
L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site:

NEW to Reeds Gap, Poe Valley, and Poe Paddy State Parks this season: A DIY Junior Naturalist program!
This Do It Yourself activity guide includes activities for all 3 of our parks. *Suggested for kids ages 7-15. Younger ages can participate with more adult assistance. This program is designed for people staying in our park(s) for many days, looking for a little extra something for the kids to do, or those who live locally and can visit the parks often. All activities will take some time to complete.
Pick up your guide at either the Poe Valley or Reeds Gap State Park offices and start on your adventures!
There are 10 total activities. 3 for each park, and a page for attending a park program. As you complete all 3 activities for a park, you can stamp your book so you know that particular park is done. Once you've completed ALL activities in the book, show your completed book to park staff at either park office to receive your prizes.
**This program will run from Memorial Day to Labor Day.
Hope to see you out there!

historyTimelineInfo:
1976: had a simple discovery worksheet. no plastic badges at the time
Before 1989:  At some point we started giving copies of a sailor's passport or paper. It was left blank in area where the child would sign their own name. It became a Jr Ranger activity.
In Jan - Feb,1988: ranger went to Grand Canyon and brought back a sample of a plastic junior ranger badge
1988: ranger there that wanted to get more educational stuff for children
1988: Using the treasure map concept, used at the City-wide Haunted Happenings event, they created a one page graphic image that was changeable. Graphics & map stayed the same over time, but questions or clues were changeable.  It was printed inhouse. It was designed to lead the reader to all parts of the historic site. Earned a passport or badge or both.
Mid 90s: switched over to a plastic junior ranger badge
Mid 90s: combined both sites as a national park
Each had their own junior ranger program
Late 90s: shipmate badges
2005:  had a program, choose from multiple badges?
2007: The NPS First Annual Junior Ranger Day was a great success and the park hopes to hold more special Junior Ranger Days.
2007: a grant for the friendship junior ranger program (Ships Mate) had a special badge
2021: small update of the junior ranger book.
2008: Junior Ranger activities engaged 142 youth.
2009: 2567 junior rangers
 2010: had 3,566 junior rangers (28% increase last year)

siteName: Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site
siteInfo:
Stop by here to pick up the site specific junior ranger books
complete the book to get a site specific badge
Their education history from 1986-2000s
Initially in the 80s the site gave card stock cards with a graphic outline of a Jr Ranger Badge. There was no activity required to earn one. Sometimes it was simply an interest expressed by the child that caused a ranger to offer it. They dealt with a lot adult themes and there was no FRIENDSHIP. Fewer buildings were available as well. The primary access point was the 1819 U.S. Custom House. There was an interactive exhibit that was very inviting to children of all ages. A reproduction "sailor's trunk" or chest. In it were clothing and tools or personal items a sailor might need at sea.
At some point we started giving copies of a sailor's passport or paper. It was left blank in area where the child would sign their own name. It became a Jr Ranger activity.
In Jan - Feb,1988, A ranger attended Ranger Skills at the Grand Canyon. It was there that a presenter introduced that ranger to the plastic badges. The ranger brought a sample and info back to SAMA.
When They returned there was a new Ranger, Mrs Nicole Shatswell. She had a masters degree in art education and was very eager to get more done for children at SAMA.
Using the treasure map concept that we used at the City-wide Haunted Happenings event, she created a one page graphic image that was changeable. Graphics & map stayed the same, but questions or clues were changeable. It was printed inhouse. It was designed to lead the reader to all parts of the historic site. Earned a passport or badge or both.
This was also the beginning time of Essex National Heritage Area.
1992 was a busy time with new (rented storefront in pedestrian mall) visitors center, and the tercentennial of the Salem Witch Trials was a huge focus with a million visitors expected.
Supervisor leaving, new one arriving and death of the park's superintendent that same year were also factors in our jr ranger program's growth.
Mr Jack Farrell wandered into the Custom House one day and soon after was teaching a class how to build a dory model. Eventually he became a seasonal park ranger. One of his many contributions was a paper dory model on stock card. It could be done on site or taken home or to special events.
Ms L. Rae Emerson as supervisor was also handling the development of programs with Lynn /Essex Heritage, and our sister park Saugus Iron Works.
They believe Saugus had created a jr ranger booklet about the same time they created a garden book. It was before SAMA as far as a booklet goes.
They often held activity events during school break weeks where the booklets could be used but included additional activities for just that day. One year They had made a pattern to make your own sailor hat and wear it as you journey through the site.
They don't recall the exact time we switched over to plastic badges but it was definitely mid 90s. In fact there was an interest In getting patches! But they proved to be very expensive in comparison to the plastic badges.
The FRIENDSHIP's construction started in 1995(?) but took longer than anticipated.
Simultaneously the new Visitors Center - our condo! came on line and Superintendent S. Kesselman was very involved with the developing heritage area. The Custom House would only be open by guided tour now as were the Derby & Narbonne Hale houses. The jr Ranger books had to utilize outdoor exhibits primarily.

combined with the Maritime in the 90s.

The former Visitor Contact Station at Saugus was remodeled and renamed the Junior Ranger Center.
2009.
Saugus received a Junior Ranger Ambassador grant that funded an SCA Intern who developed an exciting metal casting program using un-leaded pewter, as well as a tree identification program. The new Salem Junior Ranger program was “Be a Privateer,” which explored skills/tricks need to be a privateer, in- cluding tying reef and stop knots and throwing stink pots.
2009:
Saugus Junior Ranger program reached 210 youth and Salem’s Junior Ranger program reached 310 youth.
Saugus Iron Works was closed to the public from September 2006 - September 2007.

Stop by any of the two visitor centers, the entrance station or campgrounds to get the free junior ranger books.
Please note that the entrance stations and campgrounds do occasionally run out.
You can get a badge at a visitor center, at a Ranger program, from a park ranger in interpretation, or by mailing your book to the park using the address listed inside the front cover.
It takes takes about 2 hours to complete the minimum of 5 pages required plus 20-60 minutes to attend a ranger program. For all pages, a program, and at least one of the Track Trails Hike/s to be completed, it is best to plan on 4-5 hours while visiting the park over a day or two.
We have a Shenandoah Virtual Junior Ranger program online here:  www.nps.gov/articles/000/shen-virtual-jr-ranger.htm
While supplies last and during our normal operating seasons/hours, we offer some of the National Junior Ranger Activity books and badges at our visitor centers including the Nightsky Explorer and Angler and typically make them more visible during associated events and programs. You can also download these and several other books and mail in for badges or patches or download a virtual badge: www.nps.gov/kids/junior-rangers.htm
Sometimes during special events, we offer special Junior Ranger patches, badges, or stickers that coordinate with special activities or nationally recognized events like Junior Ranger Day or our Wilderness Weekend. These special patches and stickers are event-dependent and change from year to year based on a variety of factors.
We also offer a variety of other virtual and in-person learning experiences. Along with several video-based education programs and nearly 80 virtual ranger programs on our website and social media, we also provide a variety of in-person programs. Our in-person programs include Ranger programs, curriculum-based education programs and school/special group field trips, and special events.
Our Ranger programs are on a variety of themes and are talks, walks, or evening programs to include Star Parties:Ranger Programs - Shenandoah National Park (U.S. National Park Service) (nps.gov)
Our education programs are based on national and state curriculum standards and are either virtual distance learning or in-person in schools and can include in-park field trips: Education Programs - Shenandoah National Park (U.S. National Park Service) (nps.gov)
You can visit our web for ways to participate in these programs. You can follow our special events on our social media sites or our website's calendar: www.nps.gov/shen/planyourvisit/calendar.htm

:

2007: Western national parks association developed a junior ranger book for them. It is not known if the continued  the scavenger hunt at that time
2012: they totally revamped the older traditional junior ranger book(probably 2007) and went to the older scavenger hunt idea. They had laminated cards that they gave out and once completed they would give out the new junior ranger book.
2014: there was some minor changes to the junior ranger book.
2018: some minor changes to the junior ranger book
2021: did a major overhaul update of the junior ranger scavenger hunt cards (the guide you get first and carry with you) and program. They did not update the books
2021: talked about going wooded but liked the plastic badges better because they represented the ranger badges.

—Our Junior Ranger youth programming happens intermittently throughout the year, with a focus on programming in the summer. Programs generally happen up to 6 times per day between Memorial Day and Labor Day.
historyTimelineInfo:
1974: The Junior Ranger Program at Zion National Park began in 1974 as reflected in a press release in 2002 celebrating the program's 28th year in the park.
Before 2000: In the past They have offered a 2 1/2 hour program twice daily during the summer season for children ages six to twelve
2000: a junior ranger book was introduced.
2014: switched to wooden Badges
2017: Updated the junior ranger books
